about.name: Planning a tiger safari in India

intro: Tiger safaris in India are run by state forest departments, with a fixed number of vehicles allowed into each zone per drive. Popular reserves and zones sell out months ahead for peak weekends and holidays, which is why planning matters.
This guide takes you through the decisions in order. For choosing a reserve, see tiger safari in India; for the reserve system, see best tiger reserves in India.
quickAnswer: To plan a tiger safari in India, choose a reserve and season (October to June for most reserves), book safari permits early on the official state forest department portal (Madhya Pradesh allows booking up to 120 days ahead), plan four to six drives over two or three days, mix core and buffer zones, and stay close to your entry gate. Costs depend on the permit, vehicle, guide and day of the week. No safari can guarantee a sighting.
takeaways: Book safaris only on official forest department portals or through operators who use them; many look-alike websites exist.
Madhya Pradesh's portal opens bookings up to 120 days in advance; others vary.
Plan four to six drives over two to three days for a reasonable chance of a sighting.
Jeeps (gypsies) are smaller and more flexible; canters are larger shared vehicles, cheaper per seat.
Stay near your entry gate; safaris start at dawn.

items.name: 1. Choose the reserve and dates
body: Match the reserve to your travel dates and interests: Bandhavgarh or Tadoba for sightings, Kanha for all-round wildlife, Ranthambore or Sariska for easy access from Delhi and Jaipur, Kabini for leopards and elephants too. Avoid core-zone plans from July to September.

items.name: 2. Understand the zones
body: Each reserve is divided into zones or routes, entered from specific gates. Core zones are the most sought after; buffer zones are often easier to book and can be excellent. Some zones are known for particular landscapes or animals; your lodge or operator can advise.

items.name: 3. Book the permits
body: Safari permits are sold on each state's official forest department portal: for example, Madhya Pradesh's reserves on the MP Online forest portal, and Tadoba, Ranthambore and Corbett on their state forest department sites. Permits are tied to the ID used when booking, which you must carry. Book as early as the portal allows for peak dates.

facts.Good to know: Beware of unofficial sites charging extra or selling unavailable slots

items.name: 4. Choose the vehicle
body: A jeep (gypsy) carries up to six visitors plus a driver and guide and can be booked whole for privacy. Canters carry about 20 people and are cheaper per seat; they run in some reserves such as Ranthambore and at Pench's Turia gate.

items.name: 5. Decide how many drives
body: One safari is a lottery. Four to six drives over two or three days, mixing morning and afternoon slots and different zones, gives a far better experience.

items.name: 6. Book a stay near the gate
body: Stay close to your entry gate: Tala for Bandhavgarh, Mukki or Khatia for Kanha, Moharli for Tadoba, Sawai Madhopur for Ranthambore, Ramnagar for Corbett. Lodges often help with permits and naturalists.

sections.heading: What drives the cost
paras: We do not quote fixed prices because fees change each season and differ by state, zone and nationality. When comparing quotes, check what is included:

rows: Set by the state; higher for foreign nationals, sometimes higher on weekends and holidays
A full jeep costs more than a canter seat
A registered forest guide is compulsory in most reserves
Some reserves charge for professional cameras
Lodges near popular gates cost more in peak season
Private naturalists at lodges add cost but improve the experience

sections.heading: Safari timings
paras: Safaris run in two shifts: early morning, starting around sunrise, and afternoon until sunset. Timings shift with the seasons. Some reserves close one afternoon a week (Pench on the Madhya Pradesh side is closed on Wednesday afternoons, for example), and all close for certain holidays; check before booking.

sections.heading: Tips for first-timers and families
list: Book a mix of morning and afternoon drives; mornings are cold in winter.
Children are usually allowed on safaris; check age rules for canters and night stays.
Carry snacks and water; you cannot stop at will in the forest.
Enjoy the whole forest, not only the tiger: birds, deer, langurs and landscapes make a safari.
Keep expectations realistic; not every drive will have a sighting.

items.name: Couples
body: Choose a quieter reserve such as Satpura or Pench and a good lodge, and combine with a heritage stop such as Khajuraho or Jaipur.

items.name: Families
body: Choose reserves with shorter transfers and comfortable lodges: Ranthambore, Corbett, Kanha or Kabini.

items.name: Photographers
body: Plan more drives, choose private jeeps and the drier months, and read wildlife photography in India for ethics and equipment.

safety: Stay seated in the vehicle; do not stand, lean out or get off.
Follow the guide's instructions about noise and distance.
Carry the ID used for booking; permits are checked at the gate.
Do not ask the driver to break rules to chase a sighting.
packing: Neutral clothes and warm layers for winter mornings
A dust mask or scarf for summer

faqs.q: How do I book a tiger safari in India?
faqs.a: On the official forest department portal of the state that runs the reserve, or through a lodge or operator that books there. Carry the ID used for booking.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book a tiger safari?
faqs.a: As early as the portal allows for peak dates. Madhya Pradesh's portal opens up to 120 days ahead.

faqs.q: How much does a tiger safari cost in India?
faqs.a: It depends on the reserve, zone, vehicle, day and nationality. Compare what each quote includes: permit, vehicle, guide and camera fees.

faqs.q: How many safaris should I book?
faqs.a: Four to six drives over two or three days gives a much better chance than a single safari.

faqs.q: Jeep or canter: which is better?
faqs.a: Jeeps are smaller, quieter and more flexible; canters are cheaper per seat but shared and larger.
